node.label: David R. Roediger
node.date_label: The Wages of Whiteness (1991) · Colored White (2002) · Working Toward Whiteness (2005)
node.description: A labour historian who studies the historical making of whiteness and its consequences for worker solidarity. His interview explicitly acknowledges Du Bois and relates emancipation to a broader history of labour freedom without claiming race explains all working-class conservatism.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Wages of Whiteness (1991); Colored White (2002); Working Toward Whiteness (2005).

incident_edges.relationship: Relates emancipation and the eight-hour movement to broader struggles over labour freedom.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview credits Du Bois’s general-strike interpretation; no claim that emancipation mechanically caused every later labour development.

incident_edges.relationship: Examines white-worker identity as historically constructed and as a constraint on class solidarity.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes historical racialization from natural race and explicitly denies race explains everything about labour conservatism.

incident_edges.relationship: Roediger identifies Black Reconstruction as an intellectual entry point for connecting emancipation with broader labour freedom (acknowledged 2012).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The written union interview directly records Roediger’s acknowledgment, not merely its interviewer’s introduction. It does not explain his whole research programme.

incident_edges.relationship: May draws on Roediger’s account of Irish immigrants’ pursuit of whiteness when explaining changing racial boundaries and postwar mobility.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own PBS answer explicitly credits Roediger, then differentiates later immigrant cohorts and enduring exclusions. The interview does not identify which Roediger work or edition; no title is guessed and no original book is newly read. This extends the source’s previously checked employment/family passages with an explicit named conceptual resource.

incident_edges.relationship: Bederman uses Roediger’s Wages of Whiteness in explaining how white working men linked manly independence to exclusion of Black men.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Body20/n84 supports the specific contrast between white male claims to independence and exclusions shared by women and Black men. The note identifies Roediger1991; nearby Berthoff and Horton/Horton discussions have distinct claims. No independent reading of Wages of Whiteness or inference of personal affiliation.

incident_edges.relationship: Supplies Roediger with a formulation making African American family history central to the history of the working class.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Selected indexed own1993 paragraph128 expressly quotes Berlin’s1987 Gutman introduction46. Berlin mediates Gutman’s research agenda; note2 co-credits Montgomery/Gutman/Rawick interviews and retains Brody’s range-of-positions qualification. Not a claim Berlin founded Roediger’s full argument; complete article and Berlin’s original introduction unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Roediger’s whiteness studies among resources for relating immigrant ethnicity, class and racial formation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, cites Barrett and Roediger's joint Inbetween Peoples and Roediger's Towards the Abolition of Whiteness. The 2014 foreword, p. xxiii and note 4, calls critical race and working class scholarship influential, listing The Wages of Whiteness and the joint essay among examples. James Barrett and other contributors retain credit. The later retrospective is not treated as the cause of the 2004 book; originals remain unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Singles out The Wages of Whiteness among the later historical works important to his own thinking.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Kelley explicitly identifies Roediger’s book together with Linebaugh’s writings and Rediker’s contribution as especially important in the next generation of Marxist historical work. Those co-credits are retained; no assertion that Roediger coauthored The Many-Headed Hydra or uniquely supplied every race/class insight. Original book unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Roediger’s work to frame racial identity and class consciousness as intertwined rather than competing explanations.
incident_edges.evidence_note: On394 Sugrue explicitly compares Nelson with Roediger as avoiding the sterile race-versus-class dichotomy, with notes8–9 identifying books and the1993 multiple-identities essay. Saxton/Ignatiev and Nelson retain distinct credit. This positive analytical use coexists with the following criticism; original Roediger texts unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Questions Roediger’s emphasis on white workers’ agency without sufficient attention to capital and the constraints of labor markets.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The central395 paragraph explicitly includes Roediger alongside Nelson and other labor historians in an overemphasis on workers’ ability to shape segmented labor markets. Sugrue calls for employer, market and political context while rejecting deterministic economics. The named extension applies to this agency reservation; every subsequent Nelson-specific criticism is not automatically attributed to Roediger. Positive use on394 remains.

named_group_routes.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.

named_group_routes.relationship: Names Thompson among Marxist historians whose work directly shaped his own historical writing.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own answer explicitly calls these historians’ work directly formative, alongside George Rudé and later Roediger/Linebaugh/Rediker. No exact title, formal mentoring, sole method or blanket Marxist orthodoxy is inferred. E. P. Thompson is explicitly named, not Dorothy Thompson. Original works unread.
